abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for reasoning about asynchronous distributed systems under probabilistic network conditions. Traditional distributed computing theory assumes worst-case adversarial failures, which often leads to overly pessimistic bounds that fail to capture practical system behavior. We propose a stochastic fault model that characterizes network dynamics through Markov chains, enabling more precise analysis of consensus and synchronization primitives. Our framework introduces the concept of ε-synchrony, which captures the temporal correlation properties of network failures and provides a continuum between synchronous and asynchronous models. We prove that under ε-synchrony, the fundamental lower bound on round complexity for Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus can be reduced from Ω(f+1) to O(log f) when the network exhibits temporal failure locality. This represents a paradigm shift from worst-case analysis toward probabilistic reasoning about distributed agreement. Furthermore, we establish tight bounds on the trade-off between fault tolerance and message complexity under this model. Our results have significant implications for the design of distributed ledgers and blockchain protocols, where existing impossibility results can be circumvented by exploiting temporal failure patterns. We demonstrate the applicability of our framework through analysis of Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) variants under realistic network conditions.

We present significant improvements to the time and space complexity of lock-free concurrent data structures for distributed shared memory systems. Existing implementations of lock-free stacks and queues rely on double-compare-and-swap (DCAS) operations, which are not universally available on modern processor architectures. We introduce a new approach based on single-word compare-and-swap (CAS) that achieves O(1) expected time complexity while eliminating the need for complex multi-word synchronization primitives. Our method employs a novel helping mechanism that reduces contention among concurrent operations without requiring locks. We prove that our lock-free queue achieves linearizable semantics with high probability and provides wait-free progress guarantees for enqueue operations. Experimental analysis demonstrates that our implementation reduces synchronization overhead by approximately 40% compared to state-of-the-art DCAS-based approaches while maintaining comparable throughput under high contention. We also present an extension to distributed shared memory architectures that enables efficient inter-process communication with minimal coordination overhead. The theoretical contributions include new proofs of lock-free progress properties and tight bounds on the worst-case number of CAS failures per operation. This work advances the understanding of practical lock-free synchronization in distributed operating systems and provides implementable techniques applicable to real-world concurrent systems.

We present ChordLedger, a novel peer-to-peer system architecture that fundamentally reimagines the structure of permissioned distributed ledgers. Traditional blockchain systems employ monolithic consensus protocols that tightly couple ordering, validation, and execution, leading to scalability limitations and poor resource utilization. ChordLedger decouples these concerns through a hierarchical architecture consisting of micro-ledgers organized in a Chord-based overlay network. Each micro-ledger operates independently and achieves consensus among a small, fixed subset of nodes, while cross-shard transactions are coordinated through a novel two-phase commit protocol with probabilistic guarantees. Our system introduces adaptive sharding that dynamically adjusts micro-ledger composition based on workload characteristics and network topology, enabling efficient handling of fluctuating transaction patterns. We prove that ChordLedger achieves safety under Byzantine failures and provides liveness guarantees under partial synchrony. The architecture supports smart contract execution with strong isolation guarantees while enabling efficient inter-contract communication across shards. Implementation and evaluation on a 1000-node testbed demonstrate that ChordLedger achieves throughput exceeding 50,000 transactions per second while maintaining sub-second latency for cross-shard transactions. This work establishes a new paradigm for distributed ledger design that balances decentralization, security, and scalability in distributed computing systems.

This paper presents SublinearPBFT, an enhanced Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance protocol that achieves sublinear message complexity in the common case while maintaining the same safety and liveness guarantees as the original PBFT. Standard PBFT requires O(n²) messages for each consensus round, where n is the number of replicas, making it unsuitable for large-scale distributed systems. SublinearPBFT exploits threshold signature schemes with aggregate signatures to compress authentication overhead, reducing the communication complexity to O(n) in the optimistic case and O(n log n) under faulty primary detection. The protocol incorporates a novel view change mechanism that utilizes threshold signatures to achieve constant-size proof of commitment from any quorum of replicas. We introduce an adaptive authentication mode that dynamically switches between full authentication and threshold authentication based on observed system behavior, providing robustness against targeted denial-of-service attacks. Extensive evaluation on geographically distributed testbeds with up to 200 replicas demonstrates that SublinearPBFT reduces network bandwidth consumption by 65% and improves throughput by 2.3× compared to standard PBFT while maintaining comparable latency. The system has been deployed in production environments managing critical infrastructure, demonstrating practical viability. We provide complete implementation details and discuss integration challenges with existing distributed operating systems and network protocols.
